title: John Henry
description: Based on the legendary steel-driving folk hero John Henry who raced against a steam drill. The minor key gives this tune a driving, powerful quality.
notes: Feel the hammering rhythm — emphasize the downbeats like driving spikes.

title: Cold Frosty Morning
description: A signature tune of the Round Peak, North Carolina tradition, 'Cold Frosty Morning' was recorded by the Da Costa Woltz Southern Broadcasters in 1927 — one of the earliest Old-Time commercial recordings. Tommy Jarrell (1901–1985), son of fiddler Ben Jarrell, kept this tune alive for generations through his influence at the annual Fiddler's Grove festivals in Union Grove, NC.
tags: tommy jarrell, jam session, G major
notes: Tommy Jarrell learned this from his father Ben Jarrell, who recorded it in 1927. The G major setting sits comfortably in first position — great for beginners but with enough melodic interest to keep advanced players engaged. Play the A part firmly, then let the B part lift slightly. The tune pairs naturally with a banjo in clawhammer style.

title: Angeline the Baker
description: A song-and-dance tune from the 19th-century American parlor and minstrel tradition, 'Angeline the Baker' appears in mid-century song collections as a gentle courting song. The 'baker' may refer to a woman who baked bread — a common village trade. The tune was collected in both Southern and Northern fiddle traditions, suggesting it traveled widely through the 19th-century music publishing industry and itinerant dance musicians.

title: Rye Whiskey
description: A song of whiskey culture from the Appalachian tradition, 'Rye Whiskey' belongs to a broad category of drinking songs that blend humor with genuine pathos. Rye whiskey — distilled from rye grain — was the dominant spirit of the American frontier, produced in home stills throughout Appalachia. The song's modal tonality gives the comedy a darker undertow. It was collected by John Lomax, Cecil Sharp, and multiple folklorists across the Southern mountains.
notes: A song-tune with a wry, world-weary humor — 'Rye whiskey, rye whiskey, rye whiskey I cry / If I don't get rye whiskey I surely will die.' Play it with that resigned, philosophical quality. The modal scale gives it a haunted quality that goes beyond simple comedy. Many fiddlers play it slowly and deliberately, almost like a lament.

title: Leather Britches
description: A playful G major reel with a history stretching back to at least the 18th century. 'Leather britches' are dried green beans — a Southern Appalachian preservation method.
tags: ancient, appalachian, G major, folk history
notes: The B part has a distinctly different character from the A — play the contrast clearly.

title: Ducks on the Millpond
description: A gentle, unhurried Appalachian tune with a water-like quality in the melody.
notes: Focus on the smoothness of the bow — glide like a duck, don't flap.

title: Cricket on the Hearth
description: Named for the beloved hearth cricket of Appalachian mountain homes. The delicate, light bow style needed to render the crickets' chirps makes this a bow technique challenge.
notes: Use a light, fast bow close to the tip — aim for a crisp, chirping sound.

title: Black Mountain Rag
description: A Doc Watson showpiece that became one of the most imitated Old-Time guitar and fiddle pieces of the modern era.
notes: Start at half speed. The A-D-A chord motion must feel automatic before you add speed.

title: Hickory Jack
description: Hickory (Carya spp.) was one of the most valued trees in the Appalachian forest — hard, shock-resistant, and used for tool handles, wagon wheels, axles, and furniture. The name 'Jack' was a generic working-class name in American folk culture (see also 'Cracker Jack,' 'Flapjack,' 'Steeplejack'). Hickory Jack as a character represents the competent, self-reliant Appalachian worker — the backbone of the mountain economy. The tune has a similar character: reliable, sturdy, unpretentious.
notes: A solid, workmanlike breakdown — 'Hickory Jack' sounds like a character you'd want clearing timber. Play it with honest, grounded energy: no flashy tricks, just clean notes and steady rhythm. The hickory wood reference suggests hardness and durability — bring that quality to the bow arm. Great for session contexts where you want something dependable.

title: Chinquapin
description: The chinquapin (Castanea pumila) — a small chestnut native to the Appalachian understory — is now rare following the chestnut blight that began in 1900. In earlier centuries it was a food staple, medicine source, and seasonal landmark. This modal tune, distinct from 'Chinquapin Hunting,' uses a minor-pentatonic scale that predates European diatonic harmony — suggesting origins in either very old Scots-Irish tradition or Native American musical contact zones of the Southern Appalachians.
notes: A dark, modal tune — the minor pentatonic scale gives it a haunted, ancient quality. Play slowly and let the open strings drone freely. Don't rush toward the resolution; let the modal ambiguity breathe. Many players find this tune meditative at slow tempos. The chinquapin nut — small, sweet, now mostly gone — gives it an elegiac quality.

title: Nine Hundred Miles
description: A railroad song of uncertain origin that has been collected across multiple American traditions — Appalachian, blues, and labor song. The '900 miles' represents the crushing psychological distance from home experienced by itinerant workers, railroad laborers, and migrants. The Carter Family recorded it; Woody Guthrie recorded it; it appears in Lomax collections. Its wide distribution suggests it was a genuine folk song that traveled with the workers who sang it.
notes: A song-tune about a railroad journey — 'If my woman quits me, Lord, I'm 900 miles from home.' The modal quality gives it genuine pathos. Play slowly and with feeling; don't rush. The melody should feel like the endless monotony of distance. Woody Guthrie and the Carter Family both recorded versions. This is a tune that rewards simplicity over technique.

title: June Apple
description: Named for a variety of apple that ripens in early summer in the Southern Appalachians, 'June Apple' is a Mixolydian reel with roots in the mountain fiddle tradition. The Mixolydian mode — associated with Scots-Irish modal music — gives it a slightly archaic quality that distinguishes it from major-key dance tunes. It has been collected in multiple versions across Virginia, North Carolina, and Kentucky.

title: Blackest Crow
description: One of the most haunting tunes in the Old-Time repertoire. The D minor mode and slow, winding melody evoke the deep mountains and a longing that is quintessentially Appalachian.

notes: Play this slowly at first. Let the modal quality speak — don't rush the phrases.

title: Old Bunch of Keys
description: A quirky Appalachian reel with a cascading melody that sounds like keys jangling. The unusual title matches the tune's unpredictable character.

title: Lynchburg Town
description: A Virginia reel associated with Lynchburg — a center of trade and culture in the Appalachian mountain region.
tags: virginia, lynchburg, trade town, D major

title: Brilliancy
description: A showpiece Texas contest tune with flashy runs and a technical demand that explains its name.
notes: This is a showpiece tune — clean up each phrase before running them together.

title: Midnight on the Water
description: A hauntingly beautiful D minor waltz from Texas. One of the most emotionally resonant tunes in the genre.
notes: Play this with a long, slow bow and feel every note. Don't rush — let the sadness breathe.

title: Hull's Victory
description: Written to celebrate Captain Isaac Hull's naval victory over HMS Guerriere in 1812. A stately hornpipe with dotted rhythms evoking military fanfares.
notes: Play with a strong, dotted hornpipe rhythm — not too fast. Feel the military pride.

title: Salt Creek
description: A reel in the Old-Time tradition that was adopted into early bluegrass by Bill Monroe and popularized through his recordings. 'Salt Creek' — named for a tributary of the White River in Indiana — represents the crossover moment when Old-Time fiddle material entered the nascent bluegrass vocabulary. The tune's popularity on both sides of the genre divide makes it a useful bridge for musicians crossing between communities.
notes: A tune that lives at the boundary of Old-Time and bluegrass — Bill Monroe played it, which elevated its profile enormously. The bow arm needs to be relaxed but powerful; the 8th notes should flow like a stream. The B part is the technical challenge: those descending runs need to be drilled slowly before building speed. Clean left-hand articulation is key.

title: Rose Tree
description: An 18th-century English and Irish dance tune, 'Rose Tree' (also 'The Rose Tree') appears in multiple period collections including Playford's Dancing Master tradition. It was one of the tunes that crossed the Atlantic in the early settlement period, carried by British immigrants. The rose was one of the most culturally significant flowers of the European tradition — symbol of love, beauty, and brevity of life. The tune's graceful character reflects its origins in formal social dancing contexts.
notes: A courtly, 18th-century melody with a formal dignity — this tune came from a world of minuets and country dances, not barn dances. Play it with a poised, upright posture in the bow arm and clean, articulate notes. The melodic line has a floral, ornamental quality; let the phrases breathe and complete themselves fully.

title: Beaumont Rag
description: A swinging Texas rag with syncopated bow rhythms and a jazzy feel. Closely associated with Bob Wills and his Texas Playboys.
tags: texas swing, bob wills, rag, jazz influence
notes: The swing feel is everything here — don't play it straight. Let the bow bounce.

title: Hook and Line
description: A D major reel with a fishing theme — the elegant, darting phrases suggest a line cast into a mountain stream.

title: Dusty Miller
description: A tune of Scottish and Irish origin, 'Dusty Miller' references the miller whose clothes were perpetually covered in flour dust — a stock figure in British folk humor and song. Published in multiple early collections including Gow's 'Repository of the Dance Music of Scotland' (1799), it crossed the Atlantic and appeared in American fiddle books throughout the 19th century. The name was applied to various tunes across traditions, suggesting it functioned as a generic 'miller's tune.'
notes: An old tune with a courtly feel — don't rush it. The dotted rhythms in some versions suggest a mild hornpipe influence. The A part has a satisfying arc that should feel inevitable; the B part offers contrast. In Scottish tradition this is played with more ornamentation; in Old-Time settings it's typically stripped down and driven forward.

title: Faded Love
description: Bob Wills' most famous waltz. The melody is timeless — based on an older fiddle tune his father played. Patsy Cline's version made it a country standard.
tags: bob wills, western swing, waltz, patsy cline, country classic
notes: Play with a gentle, sighing bow — this is a love song.

title: Texas Gales
description: A Texas reel with a rushing, wind-swept quality. The wide intervallic leaps and fast bow strokes suggest the open prairie in a strong wind.

title: Money Musk
description: One of New England's most historically documented reels, with roots in 18th-century British dance traditions.
notes: Play with a clean, measured bow stroke — this tune demands precision.

title: Cackling Hen
description: An imitative tune that mimics the sounds of a cackling hen. A favorite for trick fiddlers and a demonstration of how Old-Time music imitates rural farm life.
tags: imitative, trick fiddling, farm life, humorous
notes: The staccato ornaments imitate clucking — play them bright and short.

title: Rocky Road to Dublin
description: A rousing Irish jig in E minor that became popular in New England dance tradition. The 6/8 rhythm is a welcome change of pace from the usual 4/4 breakdowns.
tags: jig, irish origin, em minor, 6/8, dance
notes: The jig feel is fundamentally different from breakdowns — learn to internalize the 6/8 pulse.

title: Sitting on Top of the World
description: First recorded by the Mississippi Sheiks (Walter Vinson and Lonnie Chatmon) in 1930 for Okeh Records, 'Sitting on Top of the World' became one of the most-covered songs in American music — recorded by Bob Wills, Doc Watson, Howlin Wolf, the Grateful Dead, Eric Clapton, and dozens of others. The Mississippi Sheiks were a Black string band from Jackson, Mississippi who moved fluidly between blues, Old-Time, and pop styles, reflecting the integrated musical world of the early recording era.
notes: A blues-influenced breakdown from the 1920s — the syncopation is essential. Don't play this straight; the rhythm needs to breathe and swing slightly. The lyrical version ('Was in the spring, one summer's day / When my good gal left me, she left me to stay') should be in your ear. A tune that lives at the crossroads of blues and country.

title: Billy in the Lowground
description: One of the most beloved C major tunes in Old-Time music. 'The lowground' is a low-lying field near a creek. The C key gives the tune a distinctive, warm quality.
tags: C major, uncommon key, beloved, warm
notes: The C major key requires a slightly different hand position — take your time.

title: Ida Red
description: An old song and fiddle tune that influenced Chuck Berry's 'Maybellene.' The repetitive, driving structure is hypnotic.
notes: Try to find the groove and just stay in it — this tune is all about momentum.

title: Golden Slippers
description: Written by James A. Bland (1854–1911), one of the most successful African American songwriters of the 19th century, 'Oh Dem Golden Slippers' (1879) sold over 100,000 sheet music copies within a year of publication. Bland wrote over 700 songs, including 'Carry Me Back to Old Virginny.' The fiddle tune version stripped the song to its essence and became a parade and dance hall standard across the American South.
notes: The minstrel origins of this tune don't change the fact that it swings beautifully. Play it with a light, buoyant bow — don't dig in. The verse and chorus have different feels; the chorus lifts. This tune adapted naturally into the fiddle tradition because the melody is so strong. Listen to early recordings to hear the swagger it carries.

title: New Five Cents
description: The 'new five cents' likely refers to the Buffalo nickel (Indian Head nickel), introduced in 1913, which replaced the Liberty Head design and became immediately popular for its artistic merit. The coin featured a Native American portrait on the obverse and an American buffalo (bison) on the reverse, designed by sculptor James Earle Fraser. In folk music, naming tunes for currency ('Two Bits,' 'Dollar Tune') was a common device suggesting either the tune's value or its association with pay-day celebrations.
tags: contra dance, new england, bright, clean
notes: A reel with the jaunty confidence of new money — the 1913 nickel (the Buffalo nickel) was a point of national pride. Keep the rhythm bright and forward-moving. The two-part structure is clear and well-defined; don't blur the seam between A and B. A good tune for building speed at jam sessions because the form is predictable.

title: Tennessee Wagoner
description: 'Tennessee Wagoner' first appeared in print in the late 19th century but is certainly older, referencing the wagoning trade — freight transport by horse-drawn wagon — that was central to Appalachian commerce before railroads. Wagoners were significant cultural figures: independent, hard-living, often musical. The tune's relentless forward drive captures the rhythm of a loaded wagon on a mountain road.
tags: driving, A major, bow technique, historical
notes: This tune has a confident, roadhouse swagger. The A part should feel inevitable — each phrase arrives like a wheel hitting a rut in the road. The B part offers rhythmic variation. Named for the wagoners who drove freight over Tennessee mountain passes, the tune's steady drive evokes long hauls and hard work. Keep the tempo rock-solid; this is not a tune for fluctuating tempos.

title: Aragon Mill
description: A haunting D minor tune about a textile mill closing in Aragon, Georgia. One of the great labor songs of the New Lost City Ramblers era.
tags: labor song, mill town, haunting, georgia, new lost city ramblers
notes: Play this with weight and sadness — it's a mourning song for a lost community.

title: Kitchen Breakdown
description: A Southern kitchen dance tune — the melody has a cheerful, domestic quality suggesting informal dancing in front of a wood stove.

title: Whoa Mule
description: Mule humor was a staple of Southern folk culture — the animal's stubbornness, strength, and occasional unpredictability made it a natural comic subject. 'Whoa Mule' joins 'Flop-Eared Mule,' 'Kicking Mule,' and 'Goodbye Old Paint' in the category of working-animal tunes that celebrated the central role of draft animals in pre-mechanized Southern agriculture. The mule (a hybrid of horse and donkey) was preferred over horses for farm work in the South because of its endurance and disease resistance.
notes: A comic, mule-themed breakdown with an insistent energy — the mule won't stop, and neither should the fiddler. Keep the tempo steady and the bow arm driving. The humor comes from the relentless forward motion that mirrors the tune's subject. A good session opener when you want to set a strong, clear tempo.

title: Sweet Sunny South
description: A song of post-Civil War Southern nostalgia, 'Sweet Sunny South' was written in the 1850s and achieved enormous popularity after the Civil War as a vehicle for Lost Cause sentiment. Henry Reed's LOC recording (afcreed000154) captures a Virginia fiddler's version that strips it to its essential melody. The 'Sunny South' was a complex cultural symbol — representing both genuine homesickness and the idealization of an antebellum past that obscured its brutalities.
tags: waltz, civil war, parlor, nostalgic, slow
notes: A Southern waltz with genuine tenderness — play it with a long, sustained bow and real feeling. The 'Sweet Sunny South' was a nostalgia trope in post-Civil War Southern culture: a longing for a pre-war life that was partly real, partly mythologized. Let that bittersweet quality come through. Three-quarter time should feel like breathing.

title: Forked Deer
description: Named for the Forked Deer River in western Tennessee, this reel was a staple of the Tennessee contest fiddle tradition. The Forked Deer River — named by early settlers for its Y-shaped bifurcation — runs through Gibson, Madison, and Dyer counties in west Tennessee. The tune appears in early 20th-century fiddle contest records and was widely played in the Mississippi Delta and surrounding areas.
notes: A powerful D major reel with a characteristic hook in the A part that listeners remember immediately. The 'fork' in the title is reflected in the tune's structure — phrases that split and rejoin. Keep the bow arm strong and steady; this is not a delicate tune. The B part rises and falls dramatically. At Tennessee contests this was a staple that fiddlers used to showcase their command of the bow.

notes: This is the perfect first fiddle tune. Focus on clean string crossings and steady rhythm.

title: If I Hadn't Been A Fool
Hold Old Bald While I Dance With Josie
Old Sledge
description: Old Sledge (also called Seven Up, High-Low-Jack, or All Fours) was the dominant card game of colonial and early American society, played in taverns, on riverboats, and at social gatherings throughout the South and West. The game, brought from England in the 17th century, was widely played by all social classes. Games named for cards and gambling — 'Old Sledge,' 'Poker Night,' 'Faro' — reflect the central role of social gaming in pre-radio rural entertainment culture.
tags: card game, history, G major, driving
notes: A breakdown named for a card game — 'Seven Up' or 'Old Sledge' was the most popular American card game from the 1600s through the mid-19th century. Play with the quick, decisive energy of a card player laying down a winning hand. The rhythm should be sharp and articulate, not smooth. Good tune for demonstrating clean string crossings.

title: Betty Baker (Over the Hill to Betty Baker)
Boating Up The Sandy
description: The Big Sandy River, forming the border between West Virginia and Kentucky, was a major transportation route in the early 19th century. Before roads and railroads, flatboats and keelboats moved goods along river systems throughout Appalachia. 'Boating up' the river — working upstream against the current — was grueling labor that required organized crews working in rhythm. Work songs and fiddle tunes that matched the rhythm of physical labor were a practical necessity on early American waterways.
notes: A river tune with a powerful, upstream-pulling quality — 'boating up' meant poling or pulling a flatboat against the current. Put that muscle into the bow arm. The rhythm should feel like steady, rhythmic labor. The Sandy River (probably the Big Sandy, West Virginia/Kentucky) was a major commerce route in the early 19th century.

title: Battle of Cedar Creek
description: The Battle of Cedar Creek (October 19, 1864) was a major engagement in the Shenandoah Valley of Virginia, in which Union General Philip Sheridan rallied his army from near-defeat to a decisive victory over Confederate General Jubal Early. Sheridan's famous 'ride from Winchester' — twenty miles to reach his retreating troops — became an instant legend. Civil War battles in the Shenandoah Valley directly affected the fiddle communities of the region, and the war's memory permeated Old-Time music for generations.
notes: A march-like breakdown commemorating a Civil War battle — keep the rhythm military-steady and the tempo moderate. The A part has a marching quality; the B part adds some melodic relief. Don't rush; this is a commemoration, not a celebration. Let the weight of the history come through in the playing.

title: Bye Bye My Honey I'm Gone
Caliche Creek
description: Caliche (pronounced ka-LEE-chee) is the hardpan calcium carbonate layer found just below the surface in arid and semi-arid soils across the American Southwest, Great Plains, and parts of Texas. For farmers and ranchers, caliche was a genuine obstacle — too hard to plow through, impeding drainage and root growth. Creeks flowing through caliche country had a distinctive milky appearance. The tune likely originated in the Texas fiddle tradition, which developed its own distinct character from Appalachian styles.
notes: A Southwest-inflected tune — caliche is the calcium carbonate crust that forms in arid soils of the American Southwest and Great Plains. Play with a slightly different character than Appalachian creek tunes: drier, more open, with less of the lush mountain sound. A tune that feels like a different landscape.

title: Camp Meeting on the Fourth of July
description: Camp meeting revivals were a central institution of 19th-century American religious life — outdoor gatherings lasting days or weeks where preachers, musicians, and thousands of worshippers camped together for an extended period of communal prayer and conversion. The Fourth of July was often chosen for camp meetings because it maximized attendance. The combination — patriotism and evangelical religion — captured two of the most powerful currents in 19th-century American culture and the music that expressed both.
notes: A joyful, celebratory breakdown combining two great American institutions: the camp meeting revival and Independence Day. Play it with maximum energy and enthusiasm. This tune should feel like 300 people clapping and singing in a field. Don't hold back — this is a tune about unreserved collective joy.

Brimstone
description: Brimstone — sulfur — was the scent of hellfire in the fire-and-brimstone preaching tradition of Appalachian evangelical Protestantism. The term appears dozens of times in the King James Bible, always associated with divine wrath and eternal punishment. The tune's dark modal character reflects the theological atmosphere of the Great Awakening revivals and the camp meeting tradition that swept Appalachia from the 1790s onward. Music and religion were inseparable in mountain culture.
notes: A dark, modal tune that earns its hellfire name — brimstone (sulfur) was the smell of hell and damnation in traditional Protestant theology. Don't play this bright or fast; let the modal quality and the darkness develop. A slow-to-medium tempo reveals the menacing character. Let the open strings drone and sustain freely.

title: Big Eyed Rabbit
description: Animal-themed tunes were among the most popular in the Old-Time repertoire — 'Big Eyed Rabbit,' 'Rabbit in the Pea Patch,' 'Rabbit Where'd You Get Them Long Ears' — reflecting the rabbit's prominent place in both Appalachian hunting culture and African American trickster tales (Br'er Rabbit). The rabbit was a dietary staple and a figure of folk wisdom: always watchful, always ready to run, surviving through cleverness rather than strength.
notes: A comic, animal-themed breakdown with a loose, swinging quality. The rabbit's wide eyes suggest wariness and speed — keep the rhythm quick and light. Don't dig the bow in; let it bounce. This is one of those tunes that sounds better played with a little carelessness than with excessive precision. Great for large sessions.

title: Cluck Old Hen
description: A song-tune from the Southern Appalachian mountains with origins in the call-and-response tradition of African American and white mountain communities. 'Cluck Old Hen' uses a Mixolydian-leaning modal scale that predates European classical harmony. Collected extensively in Virginia, North Carolina, and Kentucky, it was a staple of Tommy Jarrell's Round Peak repertoire and is prized for its raw, unadorned character.
notes: One of the great modal tunes of the Old-Time canon — play it raw and rough. The pentatonic scale means you can drone open strings freely. Tommy Jarrell and Fred Cockerham's duet version is the definitive recording. Don't try to make this pretty — the grittiness IS the tune. Use lots of bow pressure and let the open strings ring.

title: Cotton-Eyed Joe
description: One of the most geographically widespread tunes in American folk music, 'Cotton-Eyed Joe' appears in both pre-Civil War minstrelsy and post-war Southern fiddle traditions. The lyrics reference an itinerant worker with eye disease. John A. Lomax collected it in Texas in the 1930s. The tune diverged into regional styles: a driving Appalachian version and a more elaborate Texas contest version.
notes: The Texas contest version is much faster and more ornamented than the Appalachian version — know which one your jam group plays. The A part uses a repetitive hook that makes it easy to learn but hard to play with real drive. Keep the drone strings ringing and accent the offbeats lightly. In Texas style, add quick slides into notes.

title: St. Anne's Reel
description: One of the most widely-played reels in North America, 'St. Anne's Reel' is a point of convergence between Old-Time, Celtic, and Quebec fiddle traditions. Its exact origins are disputed — claimed by both Irish and French-Canadian traditions. It was recorded in the early 20th century by Canadian fiddlers and adopted into Old-Time through the shared dance hall culture of the 19th century.
notes: A deceptively simple tune that rewards clean, even bow strokes. Practice the string crossings in the B part slowly — they can blur at speed if not drilled. This tune crosses genre lines freely: play it in an Old-Time jam, a Celtic session, or a Quebec contradance and you'll fit right in. In Old-Time style, flatten the rhythm slightly; in Celtic style, lift it more.

title: Liberty
description: Published as early as 1788 in the New York Magazine, 'Liberty' is one of the oldest distinctly American fiddle tunes. Its name reflects the post-Revolutionary spirit, though the tune itself may have older British roots. It became a contest staple across the South and Midwest. Variations abound — some fiddle communities play it in D, others in G.
notes: A tune with enormous rhythmic drive — feel the pulse in your bow arm, not just your fingers. The A part has an ascending run that should build energy. Don't rush; keep a solid floor tempo and let the notes speak. The B part contrast is crucial: the jump up to high position should feel like a release of pressure. Doc Watson and many North Carolina fiddlers favored this one.

title: Fisher's Hornpipe
description: Composed by Johann Fischer (c.1733–1800), a German-born musician who settled in London, 'Fisher's Hornpipe' was published around 1780. It crossed the Atlantic and was embraced in New England contradance and Southern fiddle traditions alike. The hornpipe style — originally a sailor's dance — features characteristic dotted rhythms that distinguish it from reels. Thompson's 'Compleat Collection of 200 Favourite Country Dances' preserves early versions.
tags: hornpipe, dotted rhythm, english origin, widespread
notes: The defining feature of hornpipe style is the dotted rhythm — long-short, long-short. Don't rush the dots; hornpipes should feel stately, not scrambled. Fisher's has an elegance that rewards clean bow changes. The B part has a descending run that should flow smoothly. Many fiddlers add a slight pause at phrase endings in traditional style.

title: Blackberry Blossom
description: Popularized in the 1920s and 30s but likely older in origin. 'Blackberry Blossom' belongs to the category of 'decorated' tunes — its flowing melody invites ornamentation in a way that simpler breakdowns do not. The tune crossed from Old-Time into early bluegrass, becoming a vehicle for virtuosic picking. Flatt & Scruggs and later Doc Watson helped cement its place in American acoustic music.

title: Drowsy Maggie
description: An Irish reel that crossed the Atlantic and became naturalized in New England contradance music, 'Drowsy Maggie' was printed in O'Neill's 'The Dance Music of Ireland' (1907). Its name likely refers to a fictional sleepy girl — a common trope in Irish naming conventions. The tune's E minor tonality is unusual enough to make it stand out in any session, contributing to its widespread adoption across traditions.
tags: irish origin, em minor, contra dance, new england
notes: The E minor key gives this tune a darker, more introspective quality than most reels. Let the minor color show — don't rush toward brightness. The B part lifts slightly before resolving back to E minor. In Celtic style, ornament with cuts and rolls; in Old-Time style, keep it smoother with more bow drive. Works beautifully at contradance speed.

title: Flowers of Edinburgh
description: A Scottish reel from the 18th century, 'Flowers of Edinburgh' appears in Robert Bremner's 'Collection of Scots Reels' (c.1757) and later in Nathaniel Gow's publications. It crossed the Atlantic and became a fixture of New England contradance tradition, appearing in early American dance manuals. The Edinburgh reference evokes the cosmopolitan culture of Scotland's capital during its Enlightenment period.
notes: One of the most elegant reels in the Anglo-American tradition. The stately feel should come through even at speed — this is not a rough-edged breakdown. Play with a smooth, sustained bow stroke and let the phrases breathe. The B part has a particularly beautiful descending line. In contra dance settings, this tune can carry enormous energy without losing its refinement.

title: Fly Around My Pretty Little Miss
description: A song-and-dance tune from the Appalachian tradition, 'Fly Around My Pretty Little Miss' is a courtship song with roots in English and Scots-Irish balladry. The simple verse structure and dancing rhythm made it a social function staple in mountain communities. Collected in multiple versions across Virginia, North Carolina, and Kentucky, it represents the song-tune category — music that exists equally as song and instrumental piece.
notes: A song-tune, meaning the melody follows natural speech rhythm. Sing the words in your head as you play: 'Fly around, my pretty little miss / Fly around, my daisy.' This will help you phrase naturally rather than mechanically. Great for beginners because the form is clear and predictable. Pair it with a banjo for maximum Old-Time effect.

title: Over the Waterfall
description: A reel of unclear origin that has circulated widely across Old-Time, Cajun, and Celtic traditions. Its neutral melodic character — pleasant but not highly distinctive — may explain its adaptability across styles. It has been published in both American fiddle collections and Irish music compendia. The name evokes a natural image that fits the smooth, flowing melody.
notes: The key to this tune is perfectly even 8th notes — no swinging, no rushing. Let the bow flow smoothly across strings with minimal pressure. The D major setting means all four open strings are available as drones. Great for practicing smooth string crossings. In Cajun settings, this tune gets a very different treatment — slicker and more ornamental.

title: Ragtime Annie
description: A fiddle tune that absorbed the ragtime craze of the early 20th century, 'Ragtime Annie' blends the older Southern reel tradition with the syncopated rhythms of 1900s popular music. The tune represents the constant dialogue between folk fiddling and commercial music — a two-way street that shaped American music throughout the 20th century. It has been recorded by artists across Old-Time, bluegrass, and Western swing traditions.
notes: The ragtime influence is in the syncopation — feel the offbeat accents in the A part without forcing them. This should swing, not march. The B part is more straightforward, providing rhythmic contrast. Many players add a slight drag on the syncopated notes to emphasize the ragtime feel. Listen to early 1920s recordings to hear how fiddlers absorbed the era's popular music.

title: Rakes of Mallow
description: An Irish reel named for the town of Mallow, County Cork, 'Rakes of Mallow' was published in O'Neill's collections and carried across the Atlantic by Irish immigrants. 'Rakes' — young men who lived for pleasure and dissipation — were stock characters of 18th-century Irish folk humor. The tune settled into New England contradance tradition and remains a staple of sessions on both sides of the Atlantic.
tags: irish origin, contra dance, bouncy, beginner
notes: A bouncy G major reel with great forward drive. 'Rakes' in the title refers to dissolute men about town — the tune has a mischievous, light-footed character. Keep the bow near the tip for lightness in the A part. The B part has a longer sustained feel. This tune works beautifully for contradancing and was a staple of American dance halls in the 19th century.

title: Mississippi Sawyer
description: 'Mississippi Sawyer' was first documented in print in the 1880s but is certainly older. The sawyer — a submerged log that bobs up and down in a river current — was one of the greatest hazards of 19th-century river navigation. Mark Twain described their dangers on the Mississippi. The tune's powerful, forward-driving character seems to capture the rhythm of a great river. It appears in multiple Southern fiddle collections.
notes: A powerful tune with a confident, striding melody. The 'sawyer' was a floating log — or a cluster of logs — on the Mississippi that could sink a steamboat without warning. Channel that unpredictability: keep the drive steady but let phrase endings snap. The B part has a particularly strong close. This tune works beautifully at outdoor sessions and contradances.

title: Whiskey Before Breakfast
description: Despite its lighthearted title, 'Whiskey Before Breakfast' is a tune of real melodic beauty. Its origins are obscure — it appears in neither O'Neill's nor most early American collections — suggesting it may be a 20th-century composition that achieved the status of a traditional tune through widespread adoption. It has become a jam session standard across Old-Time and Celtic traditions, valued for its singable melody and clean structure.

In Celtic sessions this is played with more lift; in Old-Time sessions it's smoother.

title: Whiskey in the Jar
description: One of the oldest surviving Irish folk songs, 'Whiskey in the Jar' tells the story of an Irish highwayman betrayed by his lover. Versions appear in print from the early 18th century. It was carried to America by Irish immigrants and naturalized in the Southern mountain tradition. Metallica's 1998 cover introduced it to a new generation, but the tune's roots are firmly in 300 years of Irish oral tradition.
notes: A song-tune — let the words guide the phrasing: 'As I was going over the far-famous Kerry mountains...' The melody should breathe naturally, not march. The G major key and simple structure make this accessible for beginners, but the singing quality takes time to develop. Many fiddlers ornament the long notes with gentle vibrato or a bow accent.

title: Wildwood Flower
description: Originally published in 1860 as 'I'll Twine 'Mid the Ringlets' by Maud Irving and Joseph Philbrick Webster, the song was transformed by the Carter Family's 1928 Victor recording into the most recognizable guitar piece in American folk music. Sara Carter's rhythm guitar and Maybelle Carter's melody-lead style became the template for country guitar. A.P. Carter adapted the lyrics. The tune's journey from parlor song to country classic exemplifies the Carter Family's role in defining American vernacular music.
tags: carter family, parlor song, singable, history
notes: The fiddle version flows naturally in C major — let the melody sing. This was originally a parlor song ('I'll Twine 'Mid the Ringlets'), and that parlor sensibility should come through: refined, gentle, lyrical. The Carter Family's guitar accompaniment defined the tune's character, but the fiddle version can carry that same dignified quality. Don't rush; let each phrase settle.

title: Grey Eagle
description: An A major breakdown with deep Texas contest fiddle roots, 'Grey Eagle' appears in early fiddle contest records from the 1880s and was collected by Marion Thede in her 1967 compendium 'The Fiddle Book.' The eagle — symbol of American independence — gave the tune its proud, bright character. It was a showpiece for demonstrating high-position technique and clean string crossings at Southern fiddling contests.

Keep the A part grounded with strong downbows, then lift for the B part. This tune rewards confident playing; timid bowing makes it sound thin.

title: Yellow Rose of Texas
description: 'The Yellow Rose of Texas' was first published in 1853, attributed to 'J.K.,' and is believed to reference Emily D. West, a free Black woman from New York who may have distracted General Santa Anna during the Battle of San Jacinto in 1836. The tune became Texas's unofficial anthem and was a Civil War marching song for Confederate troops. Mitch Miller's 1955 recording sold over a million copies, cementing its place in American popular memory.
notes: Play it bright and forward — this is a marching tune at heart. The bow should feel light and lifted, not heavy and pressed. The simple four-bar structure repeats enough to allow variation: add slides on the repeats, or ornament the long notes. Great for building a steady, reliable tempo. Audiences always recognize it, which gives you confidence.

title: Big Sandy River
description: Named for the Big Sandy River that forms the border between Kentucky and West Virginia, this reel captures the rolling landscape of the region. The Big Sandy watershed was heavily settled by Scots-Irish families in the late 18th century who brought their fiddle traditions with them. The tune's smooth, rolling character evokes the river itself — wide, steady, and deep.
notes: A rolling, river-smooth reel — let the bow float through the phrases without digging in. The G major key with open strings available as drones gives it a full, resonant sound. Keep the tempo steady; this tune's character comes from evenness, not excitement. At Midwest fiddle contests it's often played with a slightly more swinging feel than Appalachian style.

title: Georgia Railroad
description: The Western & Atlantic Railroad (the 'Georgia Railroad' line) was built between 1836 and 1851, connecting Atlanta to Chattanooga and opening up the interior South to commerce. The Great Locomotive Chase of 1862, in which Union spies stole a Confederate train on this line, became one of the Civil War's most dramatic episodes. The tune captures the rhythmic excitement of the railroad age — one of the defining technological experiences of 19th-century American life.
notes: A late 19th-century tune with a locomotive feel — keep the rhythm absolutely steady, like a train on rails. The A part has a call-and-response structure; the B part is more melodic. This works well at sessions when you want to establish a solid tempo reference for the group. Don't rush the tempo; a locomotive moves at a constant speed.

title: Hog-Eyed Man
description: A sailor's song of the mid-19th century that made its way from American seaports into the inland fiddle tradition, 'Hog-Eyed Man' (also 'Hog Eye') was sung on sailing ships and collected by folklorist Carl Sandburg in 'The American Songbag' (1927). The 'hog-eyed man' — a rough, working sailor — represents the world of maritime labor culture. The tune's migration from sea to mountain demonstrates how American folk music traveled along trade routes.
notes: A song-tune with a comic, earthy character. Let the words guide the phrasing: 'A hog-eyed man is the man for me, hog-eyed man of Tennessee.' The humor should come through in the rhythm. Keep the bow light and bouncy in the A part. This was a sailor's song originally — play it with a rollicking, shipboard swagger.

title: Liza Jane
description: One of the most widely-distributed African American song-and-dance tunes, 'Little Liza Jane' appears in print from the 1880s but is certainly older. Collected by John and Alan Lomax in multiple Southern states, the song was associated with ring plays, work songs, and dance music in Black communities. It crossed into the white fiddle tradition through the shared musical culture of the rural South and became a standard of both Old-Time and early bluegrass music.
notes: A classic song-tune — sing 'Little Liza Jane' in your head as you play. The melody has a natural lift and bounce that should carry through the bow. Keep the rhythm slightly syncopated in the A part for maximum groove. This is a tune that wants to be played loud and with confidence. Great opener for a jam — simple enough for beginners, satisfying for advanced players.

title: New Ground
description: In Southern Appalachian culture, 'new ground' referred to freshly cleared land — forest converted to farmland through the labor-intensive process of felling trees, pulling stumps, and breaking sod. This was one of the defining agricultural experiences of frontier settlement. Tunes named for agricultural activities — 'New Ground,' 'Plowing Under,' 'Harvest Home' — reflect the centrality of farming to rural Southern life and the music that accompanied it.
notes: 'New ground' was the Southern term for land just cleared of trees for the first time — ready for planting. Play this with the energy of clearing that ground: forceful, purposeful, rhythmically driven. The G major setting and open-string drones give it a full, outdoor sound. A natural jam session opener because the form is clear and the rhythm is irresistible.

title: Lee Highway Blues
description: US Route 11 — designated 'Lee Highway' after Confederate General Robert E. Lee — was one of the first numbered US highways (1926), running from Washington DC through the Shenandoah Valley and down through Tennessee and Alabama. It was a major route before Interstate 81 supplanted it. The highway blues tradition reflects Depression-era experience of migration, displacement, and the search for work along American roads.
tags: bob wills, blues, swing, texas playboys
notes: A tune with a 1930s highway feel — somewhere between a breakdown and a blues. The 'blues' quality comes from the bent notes and slight drag on certain beats. Don't play it too clean; let some rawness through. US Route 11 (Lee Highway) cuts through Virginia and Tennessee — play this like you're driving it late at night.

title: Kitchen Girl
description: A reel of uncertain origin that has circulated in Appalachian and Celtic traditions, 'Kitchen Girl' evokes the social world of early 20th-century rural households where music was made in the kitchen during informal gatherings. The domestic setting — the kitchen as the social heart of the home — was a common site for music-making in pre-radio Appalachian communities. The tune was collected in multiple versions across the Southern mountains.
