title: Sourwood Mountain
description: Named for the Sourwood tree (Oxydendrum arboreum), a native Appalachian tree prized for its honey and autumn color, 'Sourwood Mountain' is one of the most widely-collected Old-Time songs. Cecil Sharp documented it in his 'English Folk Songs from the Southern Appalachians' (1917), noting its popularity across western North Carolina and Virginia. The sourwood's late-summer blooming — when mountain bees produce distinctive sourwood honey — marked a seasonal moment in the Appalachian agricultural calendar.
notes: A song-tune with a strong, singable hook. 'Chickens a-crowing on Sourwood Mountain, hey-ho-dee-dee-dee.' Keep the rhythm lively and the melody bright — this is a courting song with a good-natured energy. The A major setting gives it warmth. Many players add open-string drones on the long notes. Great for contradances and social gatherings.

title: Waterbound
description: In pre-bridge Appalachia, being 'waterbound' — stranded by a flooded creek or river — was a frequent and sometimes dangerous predicament that could last days. Mountain roads followed creek beds and crossed streams repeatedly, making heavy rains an instant barrier. The tune captures the patient waiting of someone stuck on the far bank, watching the water rise and fall. It was widely collected across the Blue Ridge and Smokies.
notes: A song-tune where the 'waterbound' refers to being stranded on the wrong side of a flooded creek — a common predicament in pre-bridge Appalachia. Play it with patient, philosophical energy; being waterbound meant waiting. The melody is gentle and flowing — let the phrases breathe. This is a tune that sounds beautiful played slowly at medium volume.

title: Wolves A-Howlin
description: Wolves were a genuine presence in Appalachian mountain life well into the 19th century, preying on livestock and occasionally threatening communities. 'Wolves A-Howlin' evokes the frontier soundscape of early settlement — the wild, unpredictable darkness beyond the cabin window. The tune was collected in the Round Peak tradition of Surry County, North Carolina, and is associated with Tommy Jarrell's modal repertoire. The last wolves in Virginia were extirpated around 1900.
tags: tommy jarrell, round peak, modal, howling
notes: One of the most evocative titles in the Old-Time canon — play it like you're hearing wolves in the dark. The modal quality (often Dorian or pentatonic) gives it a genuinely unsettling undertone. Keep the bow slow and heavy in the slower sections. Tommy Jarrell's version is the definitive reference. Don't try to brighten this up — the darkness is the point.

title: Blue Railroad Train
description: Railroad tunes were among the most popular genres in early commercial country music — the train was the defining technology of the era, connecting isolated communities to the wider world and carrying both hope and heartbreak. 'Blue Railroad Train' reflects the early 20th-century recording industry's fascination with train imagery, which appeared in hundreds of songs from the Carter Family, Jimmy Rodgers, and countless regional artists.
notes: A train tune — keep the rhythm as steady as a locomotive. The 'blue' in the title suggests a mournful quality beneath the driving rhythm. Don't rush; a train moves at a constant, powerful pace. The breakdown character suits both contest playing and informal session settings. Listen for the rhythmic 'chug' underneath the melody.

title: Chinquapin Hunting
description: The chinquapin (Castanea pumila) is a small native chestnut tree that once grew throughout the Appalachian understory, its sweet nuts harvested by both Native Americans and Appalachian settlers in autumn. Chinquapin hunting — gathering the small, sweet nuts after the first frost — was a beloved seasonal activity for Appalachian children and families. The American chestnut blight (1900–1940) killed billions of trees, including the chinquapin; many communities lost a food source that had fed them for generations. The tune carries an elegiac undertone for a lost landscape.
notes: A light, playful tune — the chinquapin hunt was a children's activity, and the music should have that carefree quality. Keep the bow arm relaxed and the rhythm bouncy. Don't over-articulate; let phrases run together naturally. Works beautifully at a moderate tempo where dancers can actually feel the groove.

title: Temperance Reel
description: The American temperance movement of the 19th century was one of the most powerful social reform campaigns in US history, culminating in Prohibition (1920–1933). Temperance groups often used popular fiddle tunes at their meetings to draw crowds, renaming them with morally improving titles. 'Temperance Reel' is one of several tunes that acquired teetotaling associations while remaining stubbornly associated with dancing and festivity.
notes: A tune whose name was borrowed by the temperance movement for anti-alcohol campaigns — play it with cheerful defiance. The reel is bright and quick, with a clear two-part structure. Keep the bow light and let the phrases bounce. Despite its abstemious name, this tune has always sounded better at a dance where someone has brought a jug.

title: Lady of the Lake
description: Inspired by Sir Walter Scott's enormously popular 1810 epic poem 'The Lady of the Lake,' set in the Scottish Highlands, this waltz rode the wave of Romantic-era Scottish cultural enthusiasm that swept both Britain and America in the early 19th century. Scott's poem was so influential that it sparked a tourism boom in the Scottish Highlands and influenced countless folk tunes, songs, and dances named for its characters. The tune circulated in parlor music collections throughout the 19th century.
notes: A graceful, aristocratic waltz — the bow should float, never dig. The 3/4 rhythm should feel like breathing, not counting. Let the phrases arc up and back down. This tune rewards a slow tempo and a long, smooth bow. It's a formal dance piece from the parlor tradition; bring some courtliness to it.

title: Granny Does Your Dog Bite
description: A nonsense song-and-dance tune from the Appalachian comic tradition, 'Granny Does Your Dog Bite' belongs to the category of humorous call-and-response pieces that were performed at square dances and play parties. Grandmother figures in Appalachian folk culture were simultaneously respected and gently satirized — their dogs (usually fierce guard dogs on mountain homesteads) were respected too. The tune's light humor reflects the social function of dance music as community entertainment.
notes: A comic question-and-answer song-tune — play it with a grin. The rhythm has a playful hitch to it; don't smooth it out. The humor in the title should come through in the music. Great for children and beginners but satisfying for experienced players who add slurs and ornaments on the repeats.

title: Paddy on the Turnpike
description: The 'turnpike' was the 19th century's principal form of improved road — a toll road, often plank or macadamized, that allowed faster travel than muddy forest tracks. 'Paddy' — the stock Irish immigrant character — walking the turnpike represented the experience of the massive Irish immigration of the 1840s–1860s. Irish laborers built many of the turnpikes, canals, and railroads they appear in. The tune blends Irish reel structure with American square dance energy.
tags: irish immigrant, contra dance, new england, history
notes: An Irish-American reel with a driving, forward energy — 'Paddy' is going somewhere and doesn't plan to stop. Keep the bow arm pushing through phrases. The turnpike setting suggests purposeful travel. This tune sits at the crossroads of Irish and Appalachian styles; either approach works, though the Old-Time version tends to iron out some of the Irish ornaments.

title: Dallas Rag
description: Dallas, Texas was a major center of commercial country and western music recording in the 1920s and 1930s. Labels including Columbia, Victor, and OKeh regularly staged recording sessions in Dallas to capture the rich musical culture of the Southwest — from Western swing to gospel to string band music. 'Dallas Rag' evokes this era of commercial folk recording when the city was a crossroads of African American, white Southern, and Mexican musical traditions.
notes: A 1920s ragtime-inflected tune with syncopation that should feel natural, not forced. The 'rag' quality comes from the rhythmic displacement — lean into the off-beats. This sits in the same sonic territory as 'Peacock Rag' and 'Dallas Rag' recordings from the early commercial era. Let the bow arm swing slightly.

title: Glise a Sherbrooke
description: Sherbrooke is a city in the Eastern Townships of Quebec, a region settled by both French Canadians and English-speaking Loyalists after the American Revolution. The French-Canadian fiddle tradition — driven by Catholic social culture, parish dances, and a rich repertoire of reels, jigs, and hornpipes — is one of the oldest continuous fiddle traditions in North America. Quebec fiddlers like Joseph Allard and Jean Carignan developed a highly ornamented, technically demanding style that influenced players throughout the Northeast.
notes: A French-Canadian reel with a distinctive gliding character — 'glise' means 'glide' or 'slide' in French. The bowing should emphasize smooth connections between notes, with strategic slurs that give it a flowing quality. This is a tune where the phrasing matters as much as the notes. Quebec fiddlers play it with a characteristic lilt that Old-Time players often approximate.

title: John Henry Blues
description: John Henry is the great American labor hero — a Black railroad worker who is said to have driven steel faster than a steam hammer at the Big Bend Tunnel on the Chesapeake & Ohio Railway in West Virginia around 1870, then died of exhaustion. The story, whether historical or mythological, became one of the most widely recorded songs in American music. John Henry represented Black workers' dignity, strength, and resistance to industrial dehumanization. Guy Johnson's 1929 study 'John Henry: Tracking Down a Negro Legend' began the scholarly inquiry that continues today.
tags: john henry, blues, folk hero, G major
notes: One of America's great folk heroes — play this with the weight and resolve of a steel-driver. The blues quality should come through in the slightly bent notes and the heavy rhythmic pulse. Don't play this light; John Henry died swinging a hammer, and the music should carry that gravity. A slow-to-medium tempo reveals the character.

title: Log Cabin Blues
description: The log cabin was the defining architectural form of American frontier settlement — built quickly from available timber, warm in winter, intimate in scale. By the early 20th century, the log cabin had become a symbol of hardy American individualism, romanticized in popular culture even as actual log cabins were being replaced by milled-lumber houses. The 'blues' suffix places the tune in the 1920s–1930s commercial folk era when 'blues' attached to traditional tunes signaled a progressive, modern sensibility.
notes: A modal blues tune that lives in a minor-tinged, open-fifth sound world. Don't rush toward the resolution; let the modal ambiguity sit. The log cabin setting suggests isolation, self-sufficiency, and the weight of frontier life. Play it slowly enough that the modal character registers. Good string crossings and clean open-string drones are essential.

title: Peacock Rag
description: The ragtime influence on Old-Time fiddling was substantial in the 1920s — Scott Joplin's rags (1899–1917) had permeated popular culture, and fiddle players absorbed the syncopated rhythms into their repertoire. 'Peacock Rag' belongs to a category of rag-influenced dance tunes that appeared in Southern and Midwestern fiddle contests of the 1920s, reflecting the era's appetite for modern, syncopated music. The peacock's flamboyant display suggested the showmanship required.
notes: A 1920s rag-influenced tune with a strut to it — a peacock spreads its tail to show off, and you should bring some of that pride to the playing. The syncopation should feel natural and hip, not mechanical. This is a tune where tone quality matters: a full, warm sound in the upper strings makes the showoff quality land.

title: Shaking Down the Acorns
description: Mast — the nuts of forest trees including acorns, hickory nuts, beechnuts, and chestnuts — was a critical food source in Appalachian agriculture. Pigs were turned into the forest in autumn to fatten on mast, a practice called pannage or 'masting.' Shaking acorns from low branches and collecting fallen mast was seasonal labor that involved whole families. The tune captures the energetic, festive quality of this autumn harvest activity.
tags: tommy jarrell, round peak, autumn, energetic
notes: A lively, physical tune with a harvest-season energy. Shaking acorns from oak trees was a genuine activity — gathering mast for pigs, making flour, or just for the pleasure of the noise. Keep the rhythm driving and the bow arm active. The tune has a slightly 'falling' quality that reflects the acorns coming down.

title: Stoney Creek
description: Stoney Creek is a community in Patrick County, Virginia, in the Blue Ridge foothills near the North Carolina border — one of the richest areas for Old-Time fiddle tradition. The region, associated with the fiddle and banjo style known as Round Peak, produced legendary players including Tommy Jarrell, Fred Cockerham, and Kyle Creed. Water features — creeks, rivers, fords, and springs — were the central landmarks of Appalachian geography, and dozens of tunes carry their names.
tags: henry reed, LOC recording, virginia, grayson county
notes: A cool, clear reel that sounds like the water it's named for. Let the bow float through the phrases with a light, liquid touch. The A part flows downward; the B part rises. Stoney Creek tunes tend to be associated with the Round Peak and Galax regions — play it with that flat-footed, grounded rhythm underneath the flowing melody.

title: Whistle Daughter Whistle
description: A traditional song-and-dance tune of British origin that entered the American folk tradition through the 18th-century immigration period, 'Whistle Daughter Whistle' belongs to the comic song category where children and parents negotiate amusingly. The whistling tradition was an important musical skill in pre-instrument rural communities — field hollers, work signals, and entertainment all relied on the whistled voice. The tune was collected in multiple American versions by Cecil Sharp and later by Alan Lomax.
notes: A song-tune with a comic premise — a daughter who won't whistle until she gets something in return. The playful, negotiating energy should come through in the rhythm. Keep it light and bouncy. The simple pentatonic melody makes it accessible for beginners while the song character gives experienced players room for storytelling.

title: Bonaparte Crossing the Rhine
description: Napoleon Bonaparte crossed the Rhine River multiple times during his campaigns (1796, 1805, 1813), transforming European political geography. His Rhine crossings were major news events that captured the imagination of ordinary people across the Western world. American fiddle tunes named for Napoleon — 'Bonaparte,' 'Bonaparte's Retreat,' 'Bonaparte Crossing the Rhine' — reflect the intense popular fascination with the French Emperor, who was simultaneously admired for his military genius and feared as a tyrant.
notes: A fast, bright reel with heroic overtones — Napoleon crossing the Rhine was a major historical event, and the tune has that grand, sweeping quality. Keep the bow arm confident and forward. The A part marches; the B part dances. A strong tune for large sessions where you need something with momentum.

title: Mississippi Moon
description: The Mississippi River — 2,340 miles from Minnesota to the Gulf of Mexico — is the great artery of American geography and imagination. Its moonlit surface appears in countless American songs, from Stephen Foster ('Beautiful Dreamer') to Mark Twain's descriptions in 'Life on the Mississippi' (1883) to Delta blues recordings. The waltz form — slower, more romantic than a reel — perfectly suits the languid, vast quality of the great river at night.
notes: A waltz with the wide, slow sweep of a Southern river under a full moon — let the bow float with maximum length and minimal pressure. The 3/4 time should feel absolutely natural and expansive. Don't rush; the Mississippi moves slowly. This is a tune where tone quality is everything — a singing, sustained sound in the upper register.

title: Hawk's Got a Chicken
description: Chicken hawks (red-tailed hawks, Cooper's hawks) were a genuine menace to Appalachian farmsteads, regularly taking chickens from the yard in the sudden, devastating strike that gave this tune its name. Farmers went to considerable lengths to protect their flocks. In the folk imagination, the hawk became a symbol of sudden loss and the unpredictability of rural life. Animal-hunt tunes — 'Fox Chase,' 'Hawk's Got a Chicken,' 'Cat's Got the Measles' — formed a whole genre of narrative fiddle music.
notes: A dramatic, predator-energy tune — the hawk's strike should be felt in the rhythm. Keep the bow arm sharp and decisive. The syncopated rhythm suggests the sudden, violent swoop of a hawk on unsuspecting poultry. This is a great uptempo showstopper. Don't smooth out the edges; the roughness is part of the character.

title: Altamont
description: Altamont is a common Appalachian place name — meaning 'high mountain' — appearing in multiple Southern states. The tune is associated with the Galax, Virginia fiddle tradition and has circulated in Old-Time and bluegrass contests since at least the mid-20th century. North Carolina and Virginia fiddlers associated with the Galax region developed a clean, driving contest style that this tune exemplifies.
notes: A fast, bright reel from the Southern contest tradition — 'Altamont' suggests elevation and clear mountain air. Keep the bow arm confident and the tempo driving. This tune rewards careful attention to bow distribution across the phrase. Good for demonstrating clean string crossings at speed. At North Carolina contests it's often played at a blinding tempo.

title: Apple Blossom
description: Apple orchards were a cornerstone of Appalachian farm economies — apple butter, cider, dried apples, and apple brandy ('apple jack') were essential preserved foods and trade goods. The brief apple blossom period in late spring, when hillside orchards turned white and pink, was one of the most celebrated moments of the Appalachian seasonal calendar. Old-Time waltzes often carry the names of natural phenomena that marked the agricultural year.
notes: A waltz with the delicate, brief beauty of apple blossoms — play it lightly and without pressing the bow. The 3/4 time should float. Apple orchards were central to Appalachian farm life, and their brief spring bloom was a celebrated seasonal event. Keep the tempo unhurried and the tone as sweet as possible.

title: Camp Chase
description: Camp Chase in Columbus, Ohio was a Union prisoner-of-war camp that held Confederate soldiers from 1861 to 1865. At its peak it held 8,000–9,000 prisoners in conditions that were desperately overcrowded; approximately 2,260 Confederate soldiers died there, mainly from disease. The camp cemetery still exists in Columbus. Tunes named for Civil War camps — Camp Chase, Camp Douglas, Andersonville — carried the weight of that experience for the communities that lost men to those places.
notes: A reflective, minor-tinged tune named for one of the Civil War's notorious Northern prisoner-of-war camps. Play it with restraint and gravity — this is a tune about confinement and suffering. The melody has a quality of quiet endurance. Let the phrases breathe and don't rush the resolution.

title: (Old) Cheat Mountain
description: Cheat Mountain in Randolph County, West Virginia rises to 4,848 feet — one of the highest peaks in the state. The Cheat River (which the mountain takes its name from) was reputedly named for its treacherous nature, which 'cheated' travelers who tried to ford it. Civil War skirmishing occurred on Cheat Mountain in 1861 in one of Robert E. Lee's first campaigns as a Confederate general. The area remained remote and wild well into the 20th century, home to a rich fiddle tradition.
notes: A mountain breakdown with a slightly deceptive quality built into its name — the Cheat Mountain area of West Virginia was wild, remote, and treacherous country. Play it with a slightly unpredictable energy. The rhythm should feel secure but not completely square. This tune rewards fiddlers who can play with confident looseness.

title: Abe's Retreat
description: Political commentary through fiddle tune titles was a long tradition in American folk music. 'Abe's Retreat' — naming a tune for Abraham Lincoln's supposed retreat from something — suggests Southern or anti-Lincoln origin in the Civil War era. Whether sincere political commentary or ironic nickname, the title places the tune in the contentious political culture of mid-19th century America. Many Civil War-era tunes used political figures' names as coded commentary on events of the day.
notes: A tongue-in-cheek political tune — 'Abe' is presumably Lincoln, and 'retreat' was the last thing Lincoln did. Play it with some irony and forward momentum. The breakdown character suits a moderate-to-fast tempo. A historically interesting tune whose title suggests it may have originated in Confederate-sympathizing communities.

title: Booth Shot Lincoln
description: John Wilkes Booth shot President Abraham Lincoln at Ford's Theatre in Washington, DC on April 14, 1865 — five days after General Lee's surrender at Appomattox. Lincoln died the following morning. The assassination shocked the nation and transformed Reconstruction policy. That this event became the title of a fiddle tune reflects how deeply it penetrated popular consciousness — and how Old-Time music encoded American history in its repertoire. The tune circulated in both Northern and Southern communities with very different emotional valences.
notes: The most historically charged title in the Old-Time fiddle canon. Play it with the weight that event deserves — an event that changed American history on April 14, 1865. The minor-tinged quality should feel somber without being melodramatic. A tune that makes audiences stop and think.

title: Bibb County Hoedown
description: Bibb County, Georgia was named for William Wyatt Bibb, Georgia's first governor (1817). Located in central Georgia with Macon as its county seat, Bibb County was part of the fertile Georgia piedmont that supported a prosperous agricultural economy. The 'hoedown' — originally a dance where participants stamped and clapped rhythmically — became a generic term for any vigorous country dance gathering. Georgia fiddle contest traditions were distinct from both Virginia and Texas styles.
notes: A Georgia breakdown with a strong, county-fair energy. Keep the bow arm driving and the rhythm absolutely steady. A hoedown was literally a dance at a farm gathering — communal, informal, and exuberant. This tune should feel like a crowd of people who've been working hard and are ready to dance hard too.

title: Bitter Creek
description: Bitter Creek could refer to several geographic features in the American West and South — there are Bitter Creeks in Wyoming, West Virginia, and elsewhere — all named because their water was alkaline, sulfurous, or otherwise undrinkable. In Appalachian folklore, 'bitter' was used to describe situations or places that were genuinely difficult — bitter cold, bitter grief, bitter labor. Old-Time tunes with austere names often preserved an unflinching honesty about the hardships of rural life.
notes: A tune with an uncompromising name — 'bitter' in Appalachian parlance meant something difficult, hard, or genuinely unpleasant. Play it with some grit and don't try to sweeten it up. The modal quality enhances the sense of hardship. A tune that tells the truth about difficult experiences without melodrama.

title: Black-Eyed Susie
description: The black-eyed Susan (Rudbeckia hirta) is a wildflower native to eastern North America — its bright yellow petals and dark center made it one of the most recognizable flowers of the Appalachian meadow landscape. In Old-Time tradition, 'Black-Eyed Susie' refers to a young woman, likely dark-eyed and attractive. The tune appears in multiple collections from across the Appalachian region and has been recorded by dozens of artists from traditional fiddlers to modern string bands.
notes: A cheerful courting tune that's one of the most widely-played in the Old-Time tradition. Keep it bright and forward. The A part has an insistent, questioning quality; the B part answers with more confidence. This tune is great for beginners because the form is clear and forgiving, but it has enough character to reward advanced players who add ornamentation.

title: Blue Goose
description: The snow goose (Chen caerulescens) has a blue-gray 'blue morph' phase that gave it the folk name 'blue goose' in many parts of North America. Migratory waterfowl — geese, ducks, herons — were important food sources and harbingers of seasonal change in Appalachian culture. The Blue Goose was also a common name for country stores and roadhouses throughout the rural South, suggesting a warm, unpretentious gathering place.
notes: A tune with the unhurried, heavy quality of a goose in flight — keep the tempo moderate and the bow arm grounded. The Blue Goose was a real bird and a real brand, and the name suggests something solid and unpretentious. Don't rush this one. Let the open string drones carry.

title: Bound to Have a Little Fun
description: 'Bound to Have a Little Fun' belongs to the category of Old-Time tunes that are essentially mission statements — announcing their purpose in the title. In the context of pre-radio Appalachian life, where entertainment had to be created rather than consumed, the determination to have fun was not trivial. Dance gatherings, music sessions, and community events were hard-won pleasures that required planning and effort. The tune celebrates that determination with unabashed joy.
notes: A tune whose title is its entire philosophy — play it with that determined, unrepentant joy. The rhythm should feel irrepressible. This is not a tune for careful, reserved playing; it's a tune for maximum enjoyment. If the bow arm isn't having fun, start over. A perfect session closer when everyone is warmed up.

title: Bull of the Woods
description: In Southern logging camp culture, the 'bull of the woods' was the woods foreman — the authority figure who commanded the logging crew and set the pace of work. Logging was one of the most physically demanding and dangerous occupations in Appalachia, and the social hierarchy of the logging camp was intensely masculine. Tunes named for logging figures and activities — 'Bull of the Woods,' 'Lumberjack Polka,' 'The Logger's Boast' — commemorated this important regional industry.
notes: A powerful, dominant-energy tune — the bull of the woods was the biggest, strongest man on a logging crew, and this tune should feel like him. Keep the bow arm heavy and confident. The rhythm should be absolutely unshakeable. A great tune for demonstrating strong tone production and a commanding presence.

title: By The Waterfall
description: Waterfalls were sacred and recreational sites in Appalachian culture — sources of water power, swimming holes in summer, and objects of aesthetic wonder. The Appalachian mountains contain hundreds of significant waterfalls, from Looking Glass Falls in North Carolina to Blackwater Falls in West Virginia. In the Romantic tradition that permeated 19th-century American culture, waterfalls represented the sublime — the overwhelming power and beauty of nature that humans could witness but not control.
notes: A meditative, flowing tune — let the bow arm mirror the water's movement. Long, smooth strokes work better than short, detached ones. The waterfall setting suggests both beauty and power; the music should have both qualities. Play slowly enough to hear the individual notes sustain and blend. A tune that rewards patience.

title: Calico Corn
description: Calico corn — also called Indian corn, flint corn, or ornamental corn — is a heritage variety of maize with multi-colored kernels in patterns of purple, red, yellow, blue, and white. It was grown by Native American peoples throughout North America and adopted by European settlers who used it for food (cornmeal, hominy), animal feed, and decoration. The autumn harvest of calico corn was a communal activity that culminated in corn-shucking parties — community events with music, food, and dancing.
notes: A cheerful, harvest-time breakdown — calico corn (multi-colored Indian corn) was both a food crop and a decorative autumn staple. Keep the rhythm bright and energetic. This is a tune for the harvest dance, played after the corn is in the crib and the hard work is done. Let the bow bounce.

title: Black Satin
description: Satin — a smooth, glossy woven fabric with a silky texture — was a luxury textile associated with formal dress, ballrooms, and high-status social occasions in 19th-century American culture. 'Black Satin' as a tune name evokes the world of formal social dancing: polished floors, fine clothes, and carefully executed dance figures. The tune's smooth melodic character suits the material it's named for.
notes: A smooth, elegant tune that should sound like its name — silky and polished. Keep the bow arm relaxed and the tone round and warm. No roughness here. This is a tune for showing off clean intonation and smooth bow changes. Play it at a moderate tempo where the elegance can register.

title: Buckskin Reel
description: Buckskin — deer leather tanned using the deer's own brain — was the primary clothing material for Native American peoples and early European frontiersmen throughout North America. Daniel Boone, Davy Crockett, and other frontier heroes were depicted in buckskin in popular imagery. By the 19th century, 'buckskin' had become synonymous with frontier self-reliance and practical craftsmanship. Tunes with frontier-clothing names — buckskin, linsey-woolsey, homespun — evoked the aesthetic of practical self-sufficiency.
notes: A frontier-energy tune — buckskin (tanned deer leather) was the quintessential clothing material of the American frontier. Play it with the direct, unadorned quality of buckskin itself: no frills, just function. The rhythm should be solid and dependable. A good all-purpose session tune that works at any tempo.

title: Cumberland Gap
description: Cumberland Gap — the natural passage through the Cumberland Mountains at the convergence of Virginia, Kentucky, and Tennessee — was the gateway for hundreds of thousands of settlers pushing west through the Appalachians in the late 18th century. Daniel Boone blazed the Wilderness Road through it in 1775. The tune, named for this frontier passage, became a symbol of westward expansion and was collected widely across the South.
notes: A natural first tune for beginners — simple structure, open-string drones, and a memorable hook. Keep the bow arm relaxed and let the open strings ring between notes. The tune sounds great at moderate speed with hard downbows on beat one. Once comfortable, try adding a drone note below the melody on the repeat.

title: Bob Wills Breakdown
description: Bob Wills (1905–1975), the 'King of Western Swing,' was born in Limestone County, Texas into a deep fiddle family. His father and grandfather were both contest fiddlers. Wills merged Old-Time Texas fiddle with jazz harmonies, jazz horns, and a dancehall groove to create Western swing in the 1930s. His band, the Texas Playboys, recorded prolifically for Columbia and Vocalion. Bob Wills was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1968.
tags: bob wills, western swing, jazz, dancehall
notes: This tune captures the essence of Western swing — a groove that floats between Old-Time fiddle drive and jazz swing feel. Don't play it dead straight; let the bow breathe slightly on the offbeats. Bob Wills' rhythm was infectious — he drove his band from the back of the stage, hollering encouragement while playing. Find that same looseness.

title: Red Haired Boy
description: Known in Ireland as 'The Little Beggarman,' this Mixolydian reel was carried to America by Irish immigrants in the 18th century and embedded itself deeply in Appalachian and Southern fiddle traditions. The lowered 7th gives it a modal quality that distinguishes it from major-key reels. It appears in O'Neill's 'Music of Ireland' (1903) and has been collected across Appalachia under dozens of names.
notes: The Mixolydian mode (natural 7th scale degree flattened) is the key to this tune's character — lean into that G-natural in an A context. Don't accidentally sharpen it into G#. The tune sits in first position throughout and works beautifully at moderate speed. In Southern Old-Time style, keep the bow smooth and singing; in Appalachian style, add more drive and grit.

title: Sugar in the Gourd
description: Sugar in the gourd was literally sweet sorghum or cane sugar stored in a dried hollow gourd — a common practice in 19th-century Appalachian households before commercial packaging. Sorghum molasses was one of the few sweeteners available to mountain families. The tune, with its pentatonic leanings and driving rhythm, was collected across multiple Southern states and represents the category of 'household item' tunes that filled the Old-Time repertoire.
notes: A pentatonic-leaning breakdown with a rhythmic hook that hooks listeners immediately. The 'gourd' is a dried hollow gourd used as a water dipper or storage vessel — a staple of 19th-century rural households. Keep the bow arm driving and let the open strings ring. The rhythm has a slight syncopation that's easy to feel once you've found the groove.

title: Bone Yard
description: A 'bone yard' in American rural parlance was either a cemetery, a place where animal carcasses were disposed of, or a junkyard of discarded machinery — all suggesting the aftermath of death and the long decomposition of material things. The name gives this Old-Time tune a memento mori quality unusual in the fiddle repertoire. Modal tunes with dark titles often preserved older folk practices of naming music for the full spectrum of human (and animal) experience, not just its bright moments.
notes: A tune with a spare, skeletal quality — play it without much ornamentation, letting the bare structure show. The modal quality and open string drones give it an austere, almost eerie feeling. Keep the bow arm relaxed but the rhythm precise. This is a tune that sounds better late at night than at midday.

title: Big Scioty
description: Named for the Scioto River (pronounced 'sy-OH-tuh') in central Ohio, 'Big Scioty' is a tune from the Midwest fiddle tradition. The Scioto Valley was one of the first regions of Ohio settled by pioneers coming from Virginia and Kentucky in the early 1800s — they brought their Appalachian fiddle traditions with them, adapting them to Midwestern contest and dance hall settings. The tune appeared in early Ohio fiddle contest records.
tags: ohio, scioto river, rolling, G major
notes: An Ohio fiddle tune with a broad, rolling character — the 'big' in the name should be in the playing. The Scioto River Valley was the heart of Ohio's early settlement, and this tune has the confident stride of a prosperous agricultural community. Keep the tempo moderate and the bow arm relaxed but firm. Works beautifully in a bluegrass or Old-Time context.

title: Breaking Up Christmas
description: In Appalachian tradition, 'Christmas' extended from December 25 through January 6 (Old Christmas or Epiphany) — a twelve-day season of visiting, feasting, and dancing. 'Breaking up Christmas' was the final community dance that ended this extended holiday, marking the return to ordinary work life. The tradition was strongest in Virginia and North Carolina; folklorist Patrick Mullen documented the custom in detail. The tune carries both the festivity of Christmas and the melancholy of its ending.
notes: One of the most evocatively named tunes in the Old-Time tradition — 'breaking up Christmas' refers to the end of the holiday season, when neighbors gathered one last time for dancing and music. Play it with the festive, slightly bittersweet energy of a party ending. A strong, driving tempo is traditional.

title: Flop-Eared Mule
description: A comic fiddle tune from the Southern tradition, 'Flop-Eared Mule' belongs to the category of animal-named tunes that were popular at 19th-century dances and social gatherings — 'Old Grey Mule,' 'Kickin' Mule,' 'Hell Among the Yearlings.' The mule was the workhorse of Southern agriculture, and its cantankerous personality made it a natural subject for folk humor. The tune's unpredictable rhythm reflects the animal's stubborn character.
tags: humorous, G major, family music, dance
notes: A humorous tune named for a mule with drooping ears — play it with that same ornery, unpredictable energy. The rhythm has a slight hitch to it; don't smooth it out too much. Great for parties and dances where the audience wants something fun. The open-string drones give it a raw, outdoor quality. Many fiddlers add a 'mule bray' ornament somewhere in the B part.

title: Lost Indian
description: Recorded by Henry Reed of Glen Lyn, Virginia for the Library of Congress in 1966, 'Lost Indian' is a modal pentatonic tune with an ancient quality that suggests Native American or very early Scots-Irish influence. The name evokes the contact zone between European settlers and Native American peoples in the Appalachian frontier. Similar tunes appear in both Cherokee and Scots-Irish traditions, raising questions about cultural exchange that musicologists continue to investigate.
notes: One of the great modal tunes — the pentatonic scale and open, spacious phrases give it a genuinely ancient feeling. Play slowly at first to feel the modal quality; don't rush toward the tempo. This tune breathes differently from major-key reels. Henry Reed's LOC recording is essential listening. Let the open strings sustain freely — the droning quality IS the tune.

title: Katy Hill
description: Associated with the Round Peak area of Surry County, North Carolina — one of the richest veins of Old-Time fiddle tradition in America — 'Katy Hill' was named for a hill near the community of Katy in the Blue Ridge foothills. The Round Peak tradition, centered on the fiddle-banjo duets of Tommy Jarrell and Fred Cockerham, is known for its powerful, heavily bowed style that became highly influential in the Old-Time revival of the 1970s.

title: Soldier's Joy
description: Documented in print as early as 1780 in Thompson's 'Compleat Collection,' Soldier's Joy may derive from an English country dance called 'The King's Head.' Laudanum (opium) was once nicknamed 'soldier's joy,' lending the tune a darker folk etymology. It spread across the American South through the 18th-century fiddle tradition and remains the most commonly played tune at Old-Time jam sessions worldwide.
